segments.line: Here's the problem with going backwards. Your
body doesn't just shrink. It un- builds.
Between age four and the start of puberty, kids grow about five to six centimeters a year. That's real.
So every midnight, you lose about two inches. Your
clothes don't fit. Your bike doesn't fit.
By day eight, you need a step stool to reach the sink in your own bathroom.
Then your bones. A newborn baby has around three hundred bones.
An adult has two hundred and six. That's real.
As you grow up, bones fuse together. Going backwards, they come apart again. Your
skull. Your hips. The bottom of your spine.
Every night, a little more of you comes undone. Your
mom buys new clothes every two days. Smaller every time.
Ellie starts wearing your old hoodies. They fit her better than they fit you now.
And then the one nobody wants to talk about. Your
brain. By age six, it's already about ninety percent of its adult size.
Before that, it grows faster than at any other time in your life. Going backwards, that means it shrinks faster too.
There's a reason most adults can't remember anything from before about age three. That's real too.
A brain that young just doesn't keep memories the way an older one does. So right now, you remember everything.
Fifteen years. Mo. Your mom. Ellie.
But a three- year- old's brain can't hold all of that.
Day eight. You're seven.
Ellie is eight. At
dinner, she cuts your food for you. At
bedtime, she reads you a story, doing all the voices, the way you used to read to her. And that night, you
realize something terrible. Your
little sister is now your big sister.
